paragraphs: The following assessments concern routine manual cutting and trimming of meat, poultry, and fish. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or responsibility for food and workplace safety.

Meat, poultry, and fish cutters focus on routine cutting and trimming with knives, cleavers, saws, and other tools: dividing large pieces into retail-ready cuts to specification; removing bones, skin, and scales; trimming defects and excess fat; weighing, labeling, portioning, and sealing packages; and cleaning tools and equipment. Work is mainly in controlled indoor environments, with prolonged standing and continuous repetitive manual work, often under cold, slippery conditions and equipment-paced production.

Entirely fictional paper-based task package, 60 minutes, with no contact with food, knives, or equipment. A: Simulated package net weight specification of 500 grams ±10 grams and a target compliant-package-weight / raw-material-weight ratio of ≥70%. These are exercise conditions only, not legal or food safety standards. B: Records show 10.0 kilograms of raw material, 7.2 kilograms of finished product, and 2.0 kilograms of trimmings. The packing list shows 14 packages of 500 grams each and 1 package of 200 grams. Scale calibration records are missing. C: The raw material batch is B17, but one package is labeled B71. The hygiene inspection is unsigned, temperature records contain no measured values, and no product temperature limits are provided. You are an observer only, without authority to process food, change labels, or release products. Calculate the recorded weight balance and both yield rates, check specification and traceability discrepancies, and list knowns, unknowns, and conditions the responsible person must verify. Do not actually process food or confirm food safety.

Reference deliverable: Recorded finished-product yield is 7.2 / 10 = 72%. Packages total 14 × 0.5 +0.2 = 7.2 kilograms. The 200-gram package fails the simulated 490–510-gram specification; recorded compliant packages weigh 7.0 kilograms / 10 = 70%. Raw material minus finished product minus trimmings leaves 0.8 kilograms unexplained; do not assume loss or byproducts. Missing calibration means weights remain unverified, and 70% is not certification of compliance. Refer B17/B71 to the responsible person for traceability evidence; do not guess and change labels. Missing measured temperatures, limits, and a hygiene signature prevent any declaration of safety or disposal. Deliver a calculation table, exception list, and blank records pending calibration, traceability, hygiene, and temperature-control checks. Wait for authorized personnel to decide rework or release under actual procedures. Do not handle knives, process food, or sign acceptance.

This page covers O*NET 51-3022.00 Meat, Poultry, and Fish Cutters and Trimmers: routine cutting and trimming of meat, poultry, and seafood by hand or with hand tools, including cutting to specification, removing bones, skin, and scales, trimming defects and excess fat, weighing and labeling, portioning and sealing packages, and cleaning equipment. Common titles include deboner, meat cutter, fish processor, and trimmer. Work is mainly in controlled indoor settings with prolonged standing and repetitive manual activity. This page excludes adjacent occupations such as Slaughterers and Meat Packers (51-3023.00) and Butchers and Meat Cutters (51-3021.00).

entries: Work inputs: Meat, poultry, and fish raw materials for cutting, product specifications and yield requirements, knives, saws, and other hand tools, weighing and labeling equipment, cleaning and disinfecting supplies, and hygiene and equipment safety procedures.

Verifiable outputs: Cuts and trimmings meeting specifications, portions labeled by weight and contents, deboned, skinned, and trimmed intermediate products, ground meat and trimmings, cleaned tools and equipment, and traceable weight and batch records.

Complete human–machine workflow: Check specifications and yield → inspect raw materials and remove defects → cut by anatomical section and debone → trim and grade → weigh, label, portion, and seal → clean tools and equipment and record batches.

paragraphs: Work reality: Among O*NET respondents, 100% report continual standing, 89% continual repetitive motions, and 86% daily time pressure. These are U.S. respondent contexts, not every team. BLS describes this constituent occupation as often working in food plants with repeated cutting in cold environments. Check specifications, raw materials, trimming boundaries, weights and labels, cleaning, and equipment safety; handle exceptions within authorization.

Environment and pace: Mainly controlled indoor environments (93% daily), with possible daily exposure to very cold or hot conditions (62%) and hazardous equipment (62%), and daily protective equipment use (85%). Continual standing (100%), repetitive motions (89%), and hand use (90%) are common. Daily time pressure affects 86%, and pace is often set by equipment speed.

U.S. O*NET 51-3022.00 covers routine manual cutting and trimming. Job Zone 1–2 is a preparation classification. Record 2025 wages and 2025–2035 employment projections separately. An occupational directory does not replace Chinese food hygiene and equipment qualification requirements.

Check first: Product specifications and yield, raw material and trimming boundaries, weighing and labeling requirements, knife and equipment safety, temperature control and hygiene procedures, and batch records and traceability requirements.

Work cycle: Check specifications and yield, inspect raw materials and remove defects, cut by section and debone, trim and grade, weigh, label, and package, then clean equipment and record batches. Do not proceed before confirming all specifications and hygiene conditions, or release products before correcting weight or label inconsistencies.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: This page covers only cutting and trimming under 51-3022.00. Slaughterers and Meat Packers (51-3023.00) handle slaughter, initial cutting, and packing; Butchers and Meat Cutters (51-3021.00) cut and display meat in retail and wholesale stores. Food and tobacco roasting equipment operators handle other processing stages. Raw material states, equipment, and hygiene requirements are not interchangeable.

Butchers and meat cutters work in retail and wholesale stores, cutting, portioning, and displaying to customer requirements. This occupation cuts and trims on processing lines to batch specifications, with different deliverables and hygiene requirements.

Slaughterers and meat packers handle slaughter, bleeding, initial cutting, and packing whole carcasses or large pieces. This occupation performs finer trimming and cutting to specification after initial cutting.

Cutting and slicing machine operators set up, operate, and tend equipment. This occupation mainly cuts and trims manually with tools, with control points in knife skills and specification consistency rather than equipment parameters.
Food batchmakers focus on recipes and batch mixing. This occupation cuts and trims meat, poultry, and fish, with control points in anatomical sections, specifications, and hygiene.

Fit signals: Start with observable work behaviors

To assess fit, consider whether you can stand for long periods and use your hands continuously, maintain precision and safety in cold and slippery conditions, repeat knife work consistently to specification, and follow hygiene and equipment procedures. Tools such as RIASEC only generate hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: Prolonged standing and repetitive manual work, steady arms and wrists, consistent cutting to specification, attention to knife and floor safety, and adherence to hygiene and cleaning procedures.

Reasons for caution: Difficulty standing for long periods or using hands repetitively, previous hand or wrist injuries, difficulty concentrating in cold and slippery conditions, or unwillingness to follow hygiene and equipment safety procedures.

Use the fictional A / B / C materials above for paper-based weight calculations, specification checks, and batch checks. Observe whether you maintain accuracy and proactively report missing information. Do not use knives, substitute materials, or real food. Results provide task experience only and do not prove practical skills or physical fitness for the job.

The O*NET interest code is RC (Realistic–Conventional): an inclination toward physical and manual activity and consistent work under procedures and standards. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality measures such as the Big Five provide no job-specific evidence for this occupation and support self-reflection only. Continue checking through actual cutting, trimming, and hygiene work experience.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and support self-reflection only.

Entry pathways and capability stages

U.S.: BLS states that the processing group typically requires no formal educational credential, though some employers prefer high school completion. On-the-job training length varies by role and employer. O*NET Job Zone 1–2 is a general preparation classification; a few days to one year must not be treated as this occupation's typical training duration.

U.S. entry mainly uses on-the-job training, with some employers preferring high school completion. China: Article 44 of the Food Safety Law requires enterprise training; Article 45 governs health management and requires annual health checks and health certificates for personnel handling ready-to-eat food. Check applicability to raw-meat roles by product, duties, and locality. Verify equipment qualifications separately.

Distinguish business licensing, employee food safety training, health management, and equipment operation qualifications. Article 45 health certificate conditions concern personnel handling ready-to-eat food; do not generalize them into a personal license for all cutters. Training certificates do not automatically confer a job or equipment authority.

Entry stage: Under supervision, practice knife handling and basic cutting, anatomical section recognition, trimming and grading, weighing and labeling. Learn hygiene and equipment safety procedures and retain process records.

Work sample: The fictional A / B / C calculation table, knowns and unknowns, exception list, and record templates for responsible personnel to check, labeled as a paper exercise without practical operations or release. Seven-day plan, 20 minutes daily: Day 1, extract specifications, weights, and batches; Day 2, recalculate 72%, 70%, and the unexplained 0.8 kilograms; Day 3, check package specifications; Day 4, check batches and missing records; Day 5, list handover items, verification conditions, and blank authorized-person fields; Day 6, correct errors against the reference deliverable; Day 7, organize the work sample, look up one target employer's requirements, and record the date. If none are found, say so honestly rather than inventing a job sample.

Next step: Check the target company's product specifications, equipment and hygiene requirements, shifts, and production pace. Verify knife skills, yield, and safe operation on a supervised real production line.

Progression to greater responsibility: With experience, handle key-section cutting and deboning, train new staff, spot-check specifications and yield, or move into quality inspection, equipment operation, or team management.

body: Editorial analysis: Trial software for batch records, weight calculations, and label checks, evaluating accuracy and review costs separately. No occupational adoption or outcome research was obtained, so no comparison is made about which stage sees adoption first. Authorized personnel remain responsible for on-site cutting and trimming, hygiene, and equipment safety.

No practice license is universally required. In mainland China, requirements depend on employers, food production licensing, and hygiene requirements.

career_risk_cards.evidence_scope: Editorial risk analysis: O*NET describes standing, repetitive motions, and hazardous equipment contexts; BLS describes knives and slippery environments.
